cues.text: It was supposed to be a normal night. Just Milo, his phone, and absolutely no plans to improve his life.
He was scrolling through videos, the ancient human ritual of doing nothing while feeling extremely busy.
Then his phone displayed something unusual. Not a message. Not an update. Something that looked… very wrong.
A strange signal slipped through his earphones. And somehow, it felt like the room itself was listening.
Milo tried to pull them out. A little too late.
And then… nothing. The kind of nothing that usually means tomorrow is going to be complicated.
The next morning, Milo woke up with a headache, a dead phone, and no memory of the weirdest part of his night.
Then he heard a voice. Not from the street. Not from the phone. From inside someone else’s head.
Please don’t die again. I just bought those plants.
He could hear thoughts. Actual thoughts. Which meant one thing: his brain had either upgraded… or completely given up.
The neighbor waved politely. Meanwhile, her mind was busy remembering groceries and negotiating with a dying fern.
Naturally, Milo did what any reasonable person would do after gaining a supernatural ability. He went outside to test it.
One person was thinking about bread. Another was thinking about a missing key. A third was apparently thinking about lunch. Humanity was not mysterious. It was hungry.
Then someone smiled at him. Milo smiled back. A perfectly normal social interaction.
Wait… why is he smiling? Do I have something on my face?
Milo suddenly became very aware of his own existence. Every step felt awkward. Every movement felt visible.
But most people were too busy thinking about themselves to study him. That’s the spotlight effect: we often imagine we’re the center of everyone’s attention.
And then he discovered something even stranger. People could say one thing… while thinking something completely different.
At a café, the cashier said, ’Have a wonderful day.’ Her thoughts were mostly about the long line and the coffee machine making a suspicious noise.
People manage the impressions they give others. They try to be polite, friendly, and appropriate. Their private thoughts, however, are not always polished.
At first, reading minds felt like having the world’s most exclusive information.
But the more people he passed, the more thoughts arrived. One after another. Then all at once.
Did I lock the door? What’s for dinner? I should call Mom. Why is that song still playing in my head?
His brain had become a browser with forty-seven tabs open… and every tab was playing audio.
The human brain filters information constantly. Attention helps us focus on what matters and ignore the rest. Milo’s new power seemed to have removed the filter.
He wasn’t just hearing people. He was trying to process too much information at the same time.
For the first time, Milo wished he could go back to not knowing.
Then he spotted a cat. Surely, a cat’s mind would be simpler.
He focused. He listened. He waited for the secrets of the universe.
The cat’s entire universe appeared to involve food, comfort, and a door that someone had failed to open.
Milo had crossed dimensions, survived a mysterious signal, and been defeated by an animal that didn’t even acknowledge him.
As the day slowed down, Milo began to understand something.
A thought is not always a belief. A passing worry is not a plan. And a strange thought doesn’t automatically reveal who someone is.
People’s minds are messy. They contain memories, guesses, fears, jokes, and random nonsense. Understanding someone takes more than collecting their private thoughts.
Real understanding comes from paying attention, asking, listening, and sometimes simply helping.
Maybe knowing everything about someone isn’t the same as understanding them. Maybe respect matters more than access.
Milo walked home, hoping the whole mind-reading thing would finally stop.
He put his phone away. No scrolling. No earphones. No mysterious signals. Just peace.
Then, from somewhere outside, he heard one tiny thought.
Feed me. And… open the door.
Milo sighed. Tomorrow was going to be a very long day.
Because apparently, even silence had a lot to say.
